entries.version: P1.3 R1/R2 Docker Restart Storm Fixes
entries.title: The trading runtime can now restart inside a container without locking itself out
entries.summary: Two separate safety checks were each making a restarted Docker trading runtime give up in under a second, which used up its restart allowance and left it stopped. Both were corrected without weakening the rule that a live owner is never displaced.
details: The first check identified the previous owner only by a process number. A restarted container always gets the same small number, so it mistook its own dead predecessor for a live owner. It now also compares the exact start time of the process, so a dead or reused number is recognised and a genuinely live owner is still never taken over.

The second check refused a restart while the previous owner's 30-second claim was still valid, and gave up instantly. It now waits, for no longer than that claim's own remaining time plus a few seconds, and then takes over only once the claim has legitimately expired. If the claim is somehow still valid at the end of the wait it stops safely instead of forcing its way in.
The shared lock file is now written in one step so a status check can no longer read a half-written file and wrongly report a failure.

Today's real Host run showed the strict check protecting the system as designed: a scheduled backup closeout that started mid-way through a 55-minute closeout was turned away rather than allowed to take over, and a later duplicate was skipped as already complete.
Docker is still not the live trading runtime. The Host runtime traded and closed out normally today and was not touched.
entries.impact: A crashed or restarted Docker runtime can recover on its own after a short, bounded wait instead of ending up stopped.

entries.title: A running trading process now keeps its ownership claim fresh even during long steps
entries.summary: The runtime's claim of ownership expires after 30 seconds but was only renewed between work cycles. Real cycles often took longer, and today's end-of-day closeout took about 55 minutes, so a perfectly healthy owner could look abandoned. A background heartbeat now renews the same claim independently of how long the work takes.
details: The heartbeat renews the same existing ownership claim, not a new one, and starts only after ownership is actually obtained.
It renews roughly every third of the claim's length, derived from the claim's own setting rather than a separate number.
It can only renew the exact claim this process holds. If another runtime has taken over, the renewal fails, the heartbeat stops for good and the process refuses to start any further work and exits.
If the claim cannot be renewed for a full claim period (for example the store is unreachable) it also stops work rather than assuming it is still the owner.
A crash stops the heartbeat with the process, so the claim lapses naturally and the bounded wait and takeover from the previous fix apply unchanged.
A step already in progress is never interrupted; only the next one is prevented.
entries.impact: A healthy owner can no longer be displaced just because one step ran long, while a genuinely dead owner is still replaced after its claim expires.

entries.title: One explicit setting now decides whether the Windows host may start live trading
entries.summary: The weekday 09:00 and watchdog Windows tasks start both the live trading process and the data collectors that feed the daily evaluation, so they cannot simply be switched off when trading moves to Docker. A single setting, TRADING_RUNTIME_MODE, now lets those tasks keep running the collectors while declining to start live trading on the host.
details: host (the default) behaves exactly as before.

docker makes the host skip only the live-trading launch, with the logged reason HOST_LIVE_START_SKIPPED_CANONICAL_RUNTIME_DOCKER. The Q10, Q11 and Q12 collectors, the opportunity engine and the macro collectors keep running, and the watchdog neither starts nor tries to recover host live trading.
Any other value also skips the host launch, so a typo can never accidentally allow a second live runtime.
Rolling back means setting the mode back to host.
The setting is configuration only: it does not inspect Docker or process numbers, and it is not an ownership authority. The ownership claim remains the only thing that decides who may trade.
The setting is not turned on yet, so tomorrow's tasks still behave as today until the cutover.
entries.impact: Trading can move to Docker without losing the data collectors, and the host can be prevented from starting a competing trading process.

entries.version: P1.3 R5 Healthcheck, Shutdown and Recovery Evidence
entries.title: Docker health now follows the real ownership claim, and restart recovery was demonstrated end to end in isolation
entries.summary: Docker's health check used to judge a runtime by the lock file's heartbeat, which is only updated between work cycles, so long legitimate cycles made a healthy runtime look unhealthy. It now follows the same ownership claim the heartbeat renews, and lock-file information is only a diagnostic. A stop request during a restart wait is also now handled safely, and a full crash-and-recovery sequence was demonstrated in an isolated Docker environment.
details: The health check is strictly read-only: it opens the ownership store in read-only mode and never acquires, renews, releases or changes anything.
It reports an explicit reason: owner, generation and remaining claim time when healthy; no valid owner, another runtime owning, or an identity mismatch when not.

A stop signal received while a restarted runtime is waiting for the old claim now makes it exit cleanly without ever taking ownership. Before this, the signal handler was installed too late and the process was simply killed.

In an isolated Docker run with the real recovery logic and a mock broker: after a hard crash and a quick restart the process stayed alive and waited, took over only when the old claim expired, and showed recovery-required until the mock broker was healthy, then went fresh and green. A second restart repeated this deterministically, and Docker's restart counter stayed at zero.
No orders were placed, the real production state and the running host process were not touched, and nothing about trading, the daily evaluation, or the order-ownership checks changed.
Not yet done: the production-state after-hours Docker test against the real paper broker, and the cutover itself. The host remains the live runtime.
entries.impact: Docker health and restart behavior are now trustworthy enough to proceed to the production-state cutover test.

entries.title: Per-intent readiness/guard evidence is persisted before broker submission; evidence-write failure fails closed
entries.summary: execution_readiness.json is only the latest mutable snapshot, so the readiness value the 2026-10-06 09:02 BUY and 09:05 SELL saw at execution time could not be proven. R6 adds an append-only, per-intent evidence record written at the readiness decision point and before intent admission and broker submission. It is evidence only and prospective only.
details: New libs/execution/readiness_evidence.py appends one JSON line per BUY/SELL execution decision to data/logs/execution_readiness_evidence/<KST day>.jsonl (O_APPEND, fsync). Existing lines are never rewritten or truncated. Each record carries a deterministic record_id (digest of the decision identity), a per-intent intent_sequence so replays of one intent stay ordered, and a record_hash over its own content; an exact duplicate record_id is detected and not written twice.

Record fields: schema_version, record_id, recorded_at, phase (readiness_guard_block | pre_broker_submit), intent_id, run_id, runtime_instance_id, ownership_generation, recovery_required, portfolio_reconciled, open_orders_reconciled, orphan_claim_count, execution_readiness_ready / reasons / computed_at, guard_enabled / guard_verdict / guard_reason, broker_submission_allowed, execution_mode, symbol, side, quantity, plus correlation (entry_reason, exit_reason, signal_source, rationale). The readiness node additionally stamps state['execution_readiness_computed_at_epoch'] (evidence metadata only; the readiness dict itself is unchanged).

Write order in execute_from_packet: readiness evaluated -> guard verdict determined -> evidence persisted -> only then intent admission and broker submission. A readiness-guard BLOCK is recorded too (broker_submission_allowed=false). The result carries execution.readiness_evidence (record_id) for intent -> evidence -> Step5C/5D -> broker order matching.

Fail-closed: if the evidence cannot be persisted for a BUY/SELL in real execution mode, nothing is admitted or submitted and the execution is blocked with reason readiness_evidence_write_failed. This applies only to this evidence contract; ordinary diagnostic logging is unaffected. If a readiness-guard block cannot be recorded, the existing block (execution_not_ready / execution_readiness_missing) is still returned unchanged.

Authority rule: the record is evidence only. It is never read back by readiness, execution, ownership, Step5C or Step5D code (pinned by tests); the in-memory readiness value and guard decision stay authoritative. Scope matches the readiness guard: BUY/SELL in real execution mode inside execute_from_packet; CANCEL/MODIFY and mock mode write nothing. Other execute_owned_order callers (skills runner / approval service, execute_order node) do not evaluate the readiness guard and are not changed.

Prospective only: nothing back-fills or fabricates evidence. For 2026-10-06 09:02 BUY (order 0015433) and 09:05 SELL (order 0021826) readiness-at-execution remains UNKNOWN (root cause: historical observability gap); both orders passed the outermost readiness guard but the in-memory value was not persisted.

No change to strategy, scoring, UEF, Step5C/Step5D semantics, ownership R1-R5, guard order or broker routing. Tests: tests/test_r6_readiness_evidence.py (30 tests) cover ready/not-ready/recovery, instance id, generation, portfolio and open-order reconciliation, evidence-before-submit and before-admission ordering, fail-closed (patched and real I/O failure), append-only/idempotent/duplicate behaviour, BUY/SELL/opening_rank1_controlled_probe/stop_loss paths, and unchanged guard/routing/Step5C/5D/strategy behaviour. The existing 749-test execution/readiness/Step5/ownership regression set passes; 8 tests in tests/test_step5b_fix4.py fail identically on the pre-R6 baseline (EXECUTION_ENABLED environment dependence) and were not touched.

Docker: the running trading-agent-live image (trading-agent-20261002:61586ae) contains neither yfinance nor R6 and was not rebuilt or restarted during market hours; a new exact-SHA image and one controlled after-hours restart follow the close. R6 live acceptance is prospective: the next real/mock order must show a durable pre-submit record that matches the intent, Step5C/5D state, broker order number and fill.
entries.impact: From the next BUY/SELL on a rebuilt runtime, the exact readiness and guard values used at the execution decision are provable after the fact, and an order can no longer be submitted without that proof being durable. Historical readiness-at-execution for 2026-10-06 stays UNKNOWN.

entries.version: R6.1 Mutation-Path Scope Fix and Atomic Evidence Append
entries.title: Every production BUY/SELL mutation path needs R6 readiness evidence; the final choke point verifies it; evidence append is interprocess-atomic
entries.summary: R6 evidence only covered the canonical execute_from_packet path. R6.1 maps every execute_owned_order caller, routes the production-capable ones through one shared pre-admission evidence helper, makes execute_owned_order itself refuse a real-mode BUY/SELL without verified evidence, and serialises evidence appends across processes. No strategy, readiness, Step5C/Step5D, UEF or broker-routing semantics changed; nothing was deployed.
details: Traced call graph of execute_owned_order: (1) execute_from_packet main BUY/SELL - R6_COVERED; (2)(3) execute_from_packet upper-limit and unfilled-order-recovery CANCEL - not new BUY/SELL exposure; (4) graphs/nodes/execute_order.py legacy node - no production caller found but BUY/SELL capable, now R6_COVERED via the shared helper plus the existing readiness guard; (5) libs/skills/runner.py order.place - reached through ToolFacade.order_execute / ExecutorAgent.execute_order from the approval flow, STRUCTURALLY_BLOCKED without an evidence reference; (6) libs/approval/service.py approve() and the ToolFacade/ExecutorAgent auto-admission - R6_COVERED when a runtime readiness_state is supplied, otherwise real-mode BUY/SELL is blocked before admission.

One shared helper libs/execution/readiness_evidence.record_pre_admission_evidence (and ApprovalService.prepare_readiness_evidence for operator paths) captures the existing authoritative readiness/guard values and persists the record BEFORE admission/Step5C/execute_owned_order. Required order: readiness/guard decision -> immutable evidence -> admission -> execute_owned_order -> broker submit. The evidence is not moved after admission.

Final mutation choke point: execute_owned_order takes readiness_evidence (a reference produced by the shared helper). For real-mode new BUY/SELL (kt10000/kt10001/ORDER_SUBMIT; CANCEL/MODIFY and mock mode excluded) it verifies the reference against durable storage (exactly one hash-valid pre_broker_submit record for the same intent, side, symbol and quantity with an ALLOW verdict, fresh within 600s). Missing -> readiness_evidence_required, invalid/ambiguous -> readiness_evidence_invalid; both fail closed with NOT_SENT before any Step5C claim and with no broker call. This grants no authority; readiness/guard decisions stay with their existing owners.

Behaviour note: operator approvals of real-mode BUY/SELL (scripts/approval_cli.py -> ToolFacade -> ApprovalService) now need a runtime readiness_state or a valid evidence reference; without one they are blocked before admission. Mock mode and CANCEL/MODIFY are unchanged.

Atomic append: the whole read -> validate/dedup -> allocate intent_sequence -> append -> fsync -> read-back verification section runs under a per-day interprocess lock (O_CREAT|O_EXCL lock file, same pattern as libs/kiwoom/token_refresh_guard.py; bounded 5s wait, stale-lock breaking, storage serialisation only). Lock timeout is a write failure and blocks submission; it never fails open. Operator override of the storage location: EXECUTION_READINESS_EVIDENCE_ROOT.

Replay contract: same intent + same attempt (same readiness computation and verdicts) -> same deterministic record_id, so concurrent or repeated writers get a deterministic duplicate answer pointing at the single stored record; a new legitimate attempt gets a new record_id and the next intent_sequence. Torn or partial writes never become valid evidence: only lines that parse and verify their record_hash count, a crashed writer's fragment is isolated on its own line, and success is reported only after the written bytes are read back and verified.

entries.version: R6.2 Evidence Is Proof, Not a Capability Token; Strict Lock Identity
entries.title: Evidence is bound to one execution attempt and revalidated against current safety state; the storage lock only breaks dead or PID-reused owners
entries.summary: Independent audit of R6.1 found two blockers: a valid R6 evidence reference could be reused for up to 600 seconds (behaving like an authorization capability token), and the evidence storage lock was broken on file age alone. R6.2 removes the age-based authorization, binds evidence to exactly one execution attempt, revalidates the current canonical owner/readiness/recovery state at the final choke point, and replaces the mtime stale-break with a strict live-owner identity lock. No strategy, readiness, Step5C/Step5D, UEF or broker-routing semantics changed; nothing was deployed.
details: R6 evidence is observational proof only. The former rule (valid ALLOW record + age <= 600 s -> execution permitted) is removed together with the 600-second constant; recorded_at remains as audit/retention data. Possessing a valid ALLOW record of any age grants nothing.

Explicit execution_attempt_id: one identity per execution attempt flows readiness/guard evaluation -> R6 evidence -> admission -> execute_owned_order -> broker submit (execute_from_packet, execute_order, and the approval/ToolFacade/ExecutorAgent/skills-runner chain). It is part of the deterministic record_id and the evidence reference together with intent_id, runtime_instance_id and ownership_generation. A later call for the same intent with a different attempt id cannot reuse old evidence; a new legitimate attempt needs new evidence.

Current-safety revalidation in execute_owned_order (no strategy or readiness recomputation): the evidence must match THIS attempt, intent, side, symbol, quantity, runtime instance and ownership generation, AND the current canonical runtime-owner row (read-only) must still show the same instance and generation with a live lease, AND the current readiness value (the caller's in-memory value, or the persisted snapshot when fresh) must still be ready, same instance/generation and recovery_required=false. Any mismatch or unverifiable state fails closed with readiness_evidence_stale/readiness_evidence_invalid before any Step5C claim and with no broker call.

Consumption contract: concurrent duplicate callers for the same attempt reference the same immutable record (same deterministic record_id, one stored line); Step5C/idempotency still allows exactly one broker mutation (tested with concurrent callers: one ACCEPTED, one NOT_SENT). Reuse of old evidence, stale-generation evidence, other-instance evidence and stale-readiness evidence are all blocked.

Documented limitation: if an operator disables the existing readiness gate (EXECUTION_READINESS_GATE_ENABLED=false) and no readiness context exists, there was no readiness ALLOW decision to revalidate; the evidence stays bound to its attempt/intent/order but owner/readiness revalidation is not applied. With readiness present it is still revalidated.

Evidence-storage lock: owner-identity contract (pid, process_start_identity, owner_token, acquired_at, host_id) built on the process-identity primitives of libs/runtime/live_loop_lock.py. A live owner's lock stays valid however old it is; a dead owner or a PID-reused owner is reclaimed through an exclusive reclaim-guard; a live pid whose identity cannot be verified, or malformed lock content, fails closed; a lock written by another host/PID namespace is never reclaimed (wait, then fail closed); release requires the exact owner token + pid + start identity. The lock is published atomically (tmp file + hard link) so readers never see a half-written lock. The mtime-only stale break is removed. The lock is storage serialisation only and has no connection to trading runtime ownership.

Critical section unchanged and verified: lock -> read valid records -> dedup -> allocate intent_sequence -> append -> flush/fsync -> read-back hash verification -> exact-owner release. A dead writer's lock is reclaimable, a torn final record is invalid, and no broker submit can proceed from an unverified record.

AST caller guard improved: the execute_owned_order caller inventory now counts direct calls, 'from ... import execute_owned_order as x', module-qualified/aliased-module calls and simple name aliases (arbitrary dynamic dispatch is out of scope). Tests: tests/test_r62_attempt_and_lock.py (30), tests/test_r61_scope_fix.py (33) and tests/test_r6_readiness_evidence.py (30) updated for the new contract. Existing tests that drive the choke point directly now supply attempt-bound evidence. The 8 pre-existing tests/test_step5b_fix4.py failures are unchanged.

Not deployed: Docker was not rebuilt or restarted. The 2026-10-06 09:02 BUY and 09:05 SELL remain READINESS_AT_EXECUTION = UNKNOWN (HISTORICAL_OBSERVABILITY_GAP); nothing is fabricated. Next: independent audit, then the after-hours exact-SHA rebuild.
entries.impact: A recorded ALLOW can no longer be replayed as a reusable authorization: it is valid only for its own execution attempt and only while the same runtime instance and ownership generation still hold a ready, non-recovering state. The evidence store cannot lose a live writer's lock to a slow-but-alive process.

entries.version: P1.3 Closeout OOM Fix, 2 GiB Limit and After-Hours Production Deployment
entries.title: The in-process closeout was OOM-killed at 1 GiB; memory use is now bounded, the container limit is 2 GiB, and f4fa335 is deployed pending live acceptance
entries.summary: The 2026-10-06 and 2026-10-07 Docker restart storms (RestartCount 23 then 43) were proven to be kernel cgroup OOM kills of PID 1 during the in-process closeout at the 1 GiB limit. The closeout loaders were rewritten to stream or project the large q9/shadow/event data (outputs identical on real data), a closeout-only cross-namespace lock guard stops a Host closeout and the Docker closeout from stealing each other's lock, 1 GiB was rejected and 2 GiB adopted after an isolated full-closeout run, and image f4fa335 (with R6.2 and yfinance) was deployed after hours. Live acceptance is still pending.
details: Root cause: the docker-desktop kernel log retained one memory-cgroup OOM kill of the python PID 1 per restart (848-1019 MiB anon RSS against the 1 GiB limit). docker inspect OOMKilled/ExitCode read after a restart was not evidence because those fields reset on every restart. The durable closeout completion marker is written only after a full success, so every restart re-triggered the same closeout until the Host fallback completed it.

Memory fix (application SHA f4fa33521c1aeed30813a2799824eed5e12a58d6): streaming reader for the ~120 MB q9_decision_windows.json; opt-in payload key projection for closeout consumers that provably never read the bulky q9 row keys; streamed operator-visibility day rows; incremental q16 folding; per-symbol rank1 loading; the evaluation lens (which spans every shadow payload since 2026-06-29) folded day by day into streaming accumulators; results released after use; per-stage cgroup/RSS logging in closeout stage events.

Output equivalence was verified against the previous implementation on real 2026-10-01/02/06/07 data (rank1 byte-for-byte across 141 files). The full 20-day rolling Q9 window was not compared against the old path; effectiveness builders were compared on 5 real days and the lens on a 9-day range.

Cross-namespace closeout lock: acquire_live_loop_lock(cross_namespace_guard=True), used only by the closeout, never reclaims a foreign-namespace (Windows vs container) lock with a fresh heartbeat; the closeout refreshes its lock heartbeat every 30 s; a stale foreign heartbeat can still be reclaimed so the Host fallback keeps working. The m13 trading lock is unchanged. Verified live: a Host attempt during the isolated Docker closeout was skipped.

Limit decision: in an isolated container with all shadow history and a 350 MiB live-loop-sized ballast, 1 GiB OOMed in the Q9 stage and was rejected; 2 GiB completed in 1381 s with exit 0, one durable SUCCESS, no OOM and fresh UEF source files (process RSS peak about 984 MiB). Production limit is now 2 GiB (--memory 2g --memory-swap 3g); compose.trading.real.yaml mem_limit is 2g. The limit is defense-in-depth, not the fix.

Deployment (2026-10-07 22:39 KST, after hours, flat book): image trading-agent-20261007:f4fa335 (revision label = the full SHA; Python 3.12.15, yfinance 1.7.0, R6.2 and the guard present) replaced the old container, which is kept stopped as trading-agent-live-pre-20261007-deploy.
